cards.title: Recovery & Load Management
cards.verdict: Readiness is 99 (prime), load ratio 0.27 (Fresh / Under-trained), HRV Below Baseline.
cards.plain: this is the decision that gates every other card: the recovery reading says how much today can hold, so it is read before the training ones
cards.action: Today is a green light: this is the session to spend on the hardest work of your week.
cards.progression: Keep the ratio inside 0.8-1.3: raise load only after a week that ended green, and back off the moment a red morning follows a hard day.
cards.guardrail: Two hard days in a row is the pattern that most often precedes a dip in HRV -- when the second morning is below baseline, make that day easy whatever the plan said.

evidence.claim: Let the morning reading decide whether today is hard or easy.
evidence.source: Vesterinen V et al. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2016;48(7):1347-1354; Manresa-Rocamora A et al. Int J Environ Res Public Health 2021;18(19):10206.
evidence.finding: Prescribing hard days by HRV produced equal or better performance than a fixed plan and fewer negative responses in vagal HRV.
evidence.caveat: Duking et al. (2021) found the performance advantage small and in some analyses non-significant; the recovery benefit is the better-evidenced half.

evidence.claim: Keep the week-on-week load ratio inside the 0.8-1.3 band.
evidence.source: Gabbett TJ. The training-injury prevention paradox. Br J Sports Med 2016;50:273-280.
evidence.finding: Sustaining an acute:chronic workload ratio near 0.8-1.3 was associated with the lowest injury risk; sharp spikes above it were not.
evidence.caveat: Contested ground. Zouhal et al. (2021) and Maupin et al. (2020) find the band plausible but the evidence inconsistent, so this app treats it as a guide rail rather than a verdict.

cards.title: Strength & Muscle
cards.basis: no resistance sessions in the last 28 days
cards.verdict: No strength session is in your own record, so there is nothing to prescribe from.
cards.plain: this card fills itself in from your first logged session, rather than guessing a routine
cards.action: Log one session -- even 20 minutes -- and the next run turns this into a real prescription.

evidence.claim: Train each major muscle group at least twice a week.
evidence.source: Schoenfeld BJ, Ogborn D, Krieger JW. Effects of resistance training frequency on measures of muscle hypertrophy. Sports Med 2016;46(11):1689-1697.
evidence.finding: When weekly volume was matched, training a muscle group twice or more per week produced more growth than once.
evidence.caveat: Total weekly volume still matters more than how it is split; frequency is the easier lever when only a few sessions happen.

cards.title: Running & Hard Cardio
cards.verdict: You ran or rode 8 minutes a week across 1 sessions (about 32 minutes each), below the 150-minute weekly floor.
cards.plain: you get about 8 hard-cardio minutes a week; the health floor is 150, and the fitness gains come from adding easy minutes rather than turning every run into a race
cards.action: Add one easy 30-minute session before the weekend. Your ratio is 0.27 (Fresh / Under-trained), which means this week has room in it.
cards.progression: Add no more than one session or about 10% of weekly minutes at a time, then hold it for two weeks before the next increase.
cards.guardrail: On a day when HRV sits below your baseline, keep the session but make it easy: that is what HRV-guided prescription buys you. Skip hard intervals outright if readiness is red.

evidence.source: Gabbett TJ. The training-injury prevention paradox. Br J Sports Med 2016;50:273-280.
evidence.finding: Sustaining an acute:chronic workload ratio near 0.8-1.3 was associated with the lowest injury risk; sharp spikes above it were not.
evidence.caveat: Contested ground. Zouhal et al. (2021) and Maupin et al. (2020) find the band plausible but the evidence inconsistent, so this app treats it as a guide rail rather than a verdict.

evidence.finding: Prescribing hard days by HRV produced equal or better performance than a fixed plan and fewer negative responses in vagal HRV.
evidence.caveat: Duking et al. (2021) found the performance advantage small and in some analyses non-significant; the recovery benefit is the better-evidenced half.

evidence.claim: Aim for 150 moderate-intensity minutes a week as a floor.
evidence.source: WHO guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour, 2020.
evidence.finding: 150-300 minutes of moderate or 75-150 minutes of vigorous activity per week is the recommended range for adults.
evidence.caveat: This is a public-health floor for health outcomes, not a performance prescription for someone already training.

cards.title: Walking & Daily Movement
cards.verdict: You averaged 6,986 steps a day over the last week, clearing 8,000 on 1 of 7 days.
cards.plain: you walk about 6,986 steps a day; the mortality curve flattens near 8,000, so the goal is consistency rather than a bigger number
cards.action: Add one 15-minute walk on your two lowest days (your weakest day was 6,200 steps on 2025-01-24). That is the shortest path to 5 days above 8,000.
cards.progression: Raise the floor rather than the average: get the weakest two days of the week above the target before chasing a new daily best.
cards.guardrail: Steps are a floor, not a training session -- do not let a long walk eat the recovery a hard session needs.

evidence.claim: Walk towards 8,000 steps a day rather than 10,000 for its own sake.
evidence.source: Paluch AE et al. Daily steps and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis of 15 international cohorts. Lancet Public Health 2022;7(3):e219-e228.
evidence.finding: Mortality risk fell with more daily steps and levelled off around 6,000-8,000 in older adults and 8,000-10,000 in younger ones.
evidence.caveat: Observational, and the plateau differs by age -- the step goal here is the 8,000 end of that range, not a hard threshold.

evidence.claim: Aim for 150 moderate-intensity minutes a week as a floor.
evidence.source: WHO guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour, 2020.
evidence.finding: 150-300 minutes of moderate or 75-150 minutes of vigorous activity per week is the recommended range for adults.
evidence.caveat: This is a public-health floor for health outcomes, not a performance prescription for someone already training.

cards.title: Hiking & Hills
cards.basis: no hiking sessions in the last 28 days
cards.verdict: No hike with a logged climb is in your record for this window.
cards.plain: hill training has no history here yet, so there is no climb to progress from
cards.action: Log one hike with elevation data and this becomes a hill-fitness plan.

evidence.claim: Judge a hike by its climb, not its distance.
evidence.source: Minetti AE, Moia C, Roi GS, Susta D, Ferretti G. Energy cost of walking and running at extreme uphill and downhill slopes. J Appl Physiol 2002;93(3):1039-1046.
evidence.finding: Metabolic cost rises steeply with gradient in both gaits, with the most economical mountain-path gradient around 0.20-0.30.
evidence.caveat: Measured on a treadmill; rough ground costs more than the same gradient on a belt.

evidence.claim: Heat fitness fades fast: it needs roughly weekly exposure to stay.
evidence.source: Daanen HAM, Racinais S, Periard JD. Heat acclimation decay and re-induction. Sports Med 2018;48(2):409-430.
evidence.finding: Five or more heat days produce stable adaptations, and without exposure end-exercise heart rate decays about 2.3% and core temperature about 2.6% per day.
evidence.caveat: Decay figures come mostly from laboratory protocols, so treat the rate as an order of magnitude.

cards.title: Sleep
cards.verdict: You averaged 7.3 h a night over the last week, carrying 1.5 h of debt, with bedtime moving about 0 minutes night to night.
cards.plain: you sleep about 7.3 hours a night and owe yourself roughly 1.5 hours this week; going to bed at the same time is worth as much as going to bed earlier
cards.action: Hold this: length and timing are both steady, so the return now comes from protecting the sleep you already get on training days.
cards.progression: Add 15 minutes to the front of the night for a week, not an hour at once -- it is the bedtime that moves, not the wake time.
cards.guardrail: Do not trade sleep for a session: the performance cost of a short night is larger than the gain from the extra training.

evidence.claim: Repay sleep debt by extending the night, not by training through it.
evidence.source: Mah CD et al. The effects of sleep extension on the athletic performance of collegiate basketball players. Sleep 2011;34(7):943-950.
evidence.finding: Several weeks of extra sleep improved sprint times, shooting accuracy, reaction time and mood.
evidence.caveat: Small sample (11 players) and self-selected extension, so the size of the effect is less certain than its direction.

evidence.claim: A steady bedtime is worth chasing even when the total is short.
evidence.source: Windred DP et al. Sleep regularity is a stronger predictor of mortality risk than sleep duration. Sleep 2024;47(1):zsad253.
evidence.finding: Across ~60,000 UK Biobank participants, sleep regularity predicted all-cause mortality more strongly than sleep duration did.
evidence.caveat: Observational: regular sleepers differ in other ways that no model fully removes.
